To talk about preparing a wedding.
Sunday, 31 August. Back in Lyon, Ioana and Julien have gathered at Madame Bernard’s, with Hélène, to start preparing the wedding. On the table: a notebook, a calendar and a tart from Sophie.
Right, my children. If you want to get married in the spring, you have to start now.
In the spring? We were thinking more of the summer…
No, Julien. I have an idea. I’d like us to get married on 3 May.
Exactly. And it’s the day Henri used to whistle your waltz. I want that day to be a happy day, for everyone.
(moved) My dear… I don’t know what to say.
Then it’s decided. 3 May. What do we have to do first?
First, you have to go to the town hall to book the date. And you have to prepare a file.
Your birth certificates, ID, proof of address… And for you, Ioana, your birth certificate has to be translated into French.
And the witnesses? How many do we need?
At least two. At most four.
I already know who I want. Hélène, I’d like you to be my witness. And Radu too, if he stops fooling around.
Me? A witness, at eighty-five? I’ll have to buy myself a hat!
And I want Karim and Madame Bernard to be my witnesses. If you agree, of course.
Agree? My boy, I’ve been waiting for you to ask me since July!

“Kuh zhuh swa”: the subjunctive of être. “Que vous soyez” = “kuh voo swa-yay”.
“Kuh zhy”: the subjunctive of aller. -aille is read “eye”, as in “travail”.
“Kuh zhuh fass”: the subjunctive of faire. Double s = voiceless s, not z.
“Kuh noo shwa-zee-syõ”: -ions in the subjunctive sounds the same as in the imparfait. Only context tells them apart.
“Fair-par”: the written invitation to a wedding (or birth announcement). The final t is silent.

The subjunctive is a mood for what is necessary, wanted, possible or felt, not for certain facts. English has traces of it (“it’s essential that he be there”), but French uses it constantly: “You must be there” = “Il faut que tu SOIS là”.
In French, the subjunctive almost always comes after “que”. If you see “il faut que…”, “je veux que…”, the next verb is in the subjunctive.
Take the “ils” form of the present, remove “-ent” and add the endings: -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent.
Good news: for -er verbs, the je, tu, il and ils forms sound exactly like the present. “Il faut que je parle” sounds like “je parle”.
Learn them by heart, especially “sois”, “aie”, “aille” and “fasse”: they’re everywhere. “Il faut que j’aille”, “Je veux que tu sois là”, “Il faut que tu fasses attention”.

Same subject → INFINITIVE, not subjunctive! “Je veux venir” (I want to come: I want, I come). But: “Je veux que tu viennes” (I want you to come: I want, YOU come). English uses an infinitive in both cases, which is where the mistake comes from.
“Il faut” + infinitive is a general rule (“Il faut réserver” = you have to book). “Il faut que” + subjunctive is for a particular person (“Il faut que vous réserviez”).

In France, only the civil wedding at the town hall is legally valid. There are no godparents (“nași”) as in Romania, but 2–4 “témoins” (witnesses) who sign the register. The traditional cake, “la pièce montée”, is a pyramid of cream puffs held together with caramel.

On Monday 15 September at nine o’clock, Ioana and Julien were waiting outside the marriage office of the town hall of the 4th arrondissement. Ioana had brought a blue binder with all the papers. Julien had brought croissants, for morale.
The clerk was a woman of about fifty, with red glasses and a very serious air. She opened her big calendar.
“So, when do you want to get married?”
“On 3 May,” said Ioana. “It absolutely has to be 3 May.”

The clerk looked at the calendar, then looked at Ioana over her glasses. “Mademoiselle, 3 May next year is a Monday. You should know that weddings mostly take place on Saturdays. On Mondays, there’s hardly anyone.”

Ioana and Julien looked at each other. A Monday. All their friends would be working. Julien would have his pupils. But Ioana thought of Hélène, and of Henri, who whistled her waltz every 3 May, even on Mondays.
“It doesn’t matter,” she said. “We want 3 May. Our friends will have to take a day off, that’s all.”
The clerk sighed. “As you wish. You need to fill in these forms. Your witnesses must be adults and must have ID. And the complete file must be submitted at least one month before the date.”
She began to write their names. “Popescu, Ioana… and Moreau, Julien.” Then she stopped. She looked up. “Moreau? Julien Moreau? Are you a music teacher?”

The clerk’s face changed completely. She smiled for the first time. “You’re my son Théo’s teacher! He’s twelve. He used to hate music. Now he plays the piano every evening. He talks about you all the time!”

Julien blushed. Ioana laughed. And the clerk added, in a low voice: “Listen. On 3 May I don’t normally work. But I want to be the one who prepares your wedding. And I’m going to ask the deputy mayor to come specially. She’s a friend.”
“And could Théo play something at the end of the ceremony?” asked Julien. The clerk had tears in her eyes. “He’d be the happiest child in Lyon.”

Leaving the town hall, Julien called his parents in Annecy. His mother, Brigitte, shouted so loudly that Ioana heard her from two metres away. “3 May? A Monday? I don’t care! I have to find a dress! Pierre, you have to make the bread for the meal!”
Behind her, you could hear Manon: “And I want to sing! You have to let me sing, Julien!” And Pompon was barking, without knowing why, but with great enthusiasm.

The next day at the office, Ioana told Karim the date. “A Monday? Perfect! Nathalie will have to close the studio that day.” Nathalie, who happened to be walking down the corridor, answered without stopping: “The studio will be closed. But you have to invite me. And I want there to be champagne.”
On Wednesday, Julien told Hélène the story. She laughed for a long time. “A Monday! Henri would have loved it. He always said that Mondays deserved a little happiness too.”

As for Madame Bernard, she immediately opened her notebook. “Right. I have to let Isabelle know, so she can take a day off. Sophie has to make the pièce montée. And Victor has to have a bow tie.” On the sofa, Victor didn’t look at all convinced.
That evening, Ioana wrote in her notebook: “3 May. A Monday. The most beautiful Monday in the world.”

My dear Ioana, here is what you have to do before 3 May. Keep this list on the fridge!
In September: you have to go to the town hall of the 4th arrondissement to book the date. Don’t delay, spring is very popular.
In October: your birth certificate has to be translated by an official translator. Ask your mother to send it to you from Iași.
In November: you have to choose a venue for the party. I know a restaurant on the banks of the Saône, with a terrace.
In January: you have to send the invitations. I want Julien to write the addresses: he has the most beautiful handwriting.
In March: you have to find your dress. I’d love to come with you, if you’d like.
